title: Application Insights Distributed Tracing
description: Use Azure Application Insights to collect distributed traces across services, correlate requests with dependency calls, and diagnose slow operations in production.

data.text: When your application spans multiple services, databases, and third-party APIs, debugging a slow request can feel like solving a puzzle with missing pieces. **Azure Application Insights** collects telemetry from each component and stitches it together using distributed tracing. The result is an end-to-end view of a single request, showing exactly where time was spent and which dependency failed.

Distributed tracing in Application Insights is built on the W3C Trace Context standard. Each incoming request receives a unique trace ID, and every outgoing call carries that ID forward in HTTP headers. Application Insights automatically captures this data for ASP.NET Core, Azure Functions, Service Bus, and many common dependencies.

data.title: Key tracing concepts in Application Insights
items: Trace ID: A unique identifier for the entire end-to-end request flow across services.
Span: A single unit of work within a trace, such as an HTTP call, database query, or dependency request.
Operation ID: In Application Insights, this maps to the trace ID and links all telemetry items for one request.
Parent ID: Identifies the span that initiated the current span, enabling hierarchical visualization.
Sampling: A strategy to reduce telemetry volume by recording only a percentage of requests while still preserving accurate latency data.

data.text: Enabling Distributed Tracing in ASP.NET Core

The easiest way to enable distributed tracing is through the Application Insights SDK. Once installed, it automatically collects requests, dependencies, exceptions, and traces. You can also enable it through Azure Monitor Application Insights without code changes using the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry-based distribution.

data.title: Program.cs setup with Application Insights
data.content: Register the Application Insights SDK and enable correlation for outgoing HTTP calls.

data.text: Viewing Traces in the Azure Portal

Once telemetry is flowing, you can view distributed traces in the Azure portal under Application Insights. The **end-to-end transaction view** shows each request, its dependencies, and their durations in a flame graph. You can filter by operation name, duration, or failure status to find slow or failing requests quickly.

data.title: Application Map
data.text: The Application Map visualizes the relationships between your services. Nodes represent components, and edges represent dependency calls. The thickness and color of edges indicate call volume and failure rate, making it easy to spot problematic dependencies at a glance.

Application Insights charges by data volume, so sampling is essential for cost control. Adaptive sampling automatically adjusts the sampling percentage based on traffic volume, keeping data within your target while preserving representative traces. For high-traffic APIs, you can also configure fixed-rate sampling or exclude low-value endpoints like health checks.

data.title: Configuring adaptive sampling
data.content: Adjust sampling settings in Program.cs or appsettings.json to control telemetry volume.

terms.definition: An Azure service that collects application telemetry including requests, dependencies, exceptions, and traces for monitoring and diagnostics.
A standard for propagating trace IDs across service boundaries using HTTP headers, enabling end-to-end distributed tracing.
A telemetry sampling technique that automatically adjusts the percentage of requests recorded based on traffic volume to stay within data limits.
Linking telemetry items together using shared identifiers so you can reconstruct the full request path across services.

data.title: Distributed tracing best practices in Azure
items: Enable W3C Trace Context propagation to ensure compatibility with other tools and languages.
Instrument all outgoing HTTP, SQL, and Service Bus calls so dependencies appear in traces automatically.
Configure sampling before you reach your data cap; it is easier to reduce volume than to recover from overages.
Always keep exceptions and failed requests unsampled so you can diagnose errors.
Use the Application Map and end-to-end views during incidents, not just for routine monitoring.

items.question: What is the difference between Application Insights traces and logs?
items.answer: Application Insights traces are structured request and dependency telemetry automatically collected by the SDK. Logs are free-form messages you emit with ILogger. Traces are best for understanding request flow and latency; logs are best for detailed debugging and audit trails. Both appear in the same Application Insights resource.

items.question: Does Application Insights support OpenTelemetry?
items.answer: Yes. Azure Monitor provides an OpenTelemetry-based distribution that exports traces, metrics, and logs to Application Insights using the OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP). This lets you use one instrumentation layer across Azure and non-Azure services.

data.title: Lesson Summary
points: Application Insights collects distributed traces by correlating telemetry with trace IDs across services.
The SDK automatically instruments ASP.NET Core requests, HTTP dependencies, SQL calls, and more.
The end-to-end transaction view and Application Map help you find slow or failing dependencies quickly.
Adaptive sampling controls data volume and cost while preserving statistically representative traces.
W3C Trace Context ensures your traces work across languages, frameworks, and Azure services.
data.takeaway: Application Insights turns a scattered set of logs and metrics into a coherent story of how a request flows through your system. The faster you can read that story, the faster you can fix production issues.
